title: PACE-dLLM: Elastic Block Decoding via Confidence Cliff Estimation for Diffusion Language Models
claim: Prior methods set adaptive block sizes from indirect heuristic signals; ours reads the model's own confidence cliff, which varies with difficulty.
layout: Top row of 3 plots, bottom row baselines vs ours, left-to-right
description: The figure has three sections. Section 1 (top) shows three confidence-versus-position curves with shaded bands, for hard numeric reasoning, medium general text and easy common collocations. Each has a token strip colored by confidence (green high, yellow low, red very low, then a masked token). The curves are a steep drop, a moderate drop and a flat curve, all crossing or staying above a dashed commit-threshold line. Section 2 (bottom left, red tint) shows three baseline cards for punctuation delimiters, volatility bands and influence scores. Each card has a flag on a node line and a short note on its weakness. A large 'V S.' separates it from Section 3 (bottom right, blue tint). Section 3 shows ours as three boxed steps joined by arrows: observe the cliff, fit it and read off the saturation point h*, then set the next horizon and commit tokens. A lightbulb footer summarizes the benefit.
caption: Overview of PACE-dLLM. Top: confidence cliffs vary with local difficulty, from steep numerical-reasoning profiles to shallow collocations. Bottom: PACE estimates the next horizon from this profile and commits tokens with a separate threshold. Both decisions reuse the current forward pass; no auxiliary network or additional model pass is required.
abstract: Diffusion language models (dLLMs), such as LLaDA and Dream, have become competitive with autoregressive (AR) LLMs in generation quality while supporting native parallel decoding. A standard acceleration strategy is block-wise decoding, where each forward pass predicts a block of length B and commits high-confidence tokens. Confidence-threshold commitment adapts which tokens are accepted, but a fixed B still constrains the prediction scope. Existing horizon policies use manually chosen sizes, volatility statistics, or candidate-boundary scores. We instead use the model's own per-step confidence: in-window confidence typically follows a context-dependent cliff, providing a direct signal for adapting the look-ahead horizon. In this work, we propose PACE-dLLM, which refits this parametric cliff periodically in closed form, sets the next horizon at a shared confidence anchor, and retains confidence-threshold token commitment. Under a saturated-yield abstraction with iid, policy-independent monotone profiles, the oracle horizon is the smallest attaining maximal per-pass yield and improves the asymptotic forward-pass rate when fixed blocks undershoot it with positive probability. On four reasoning and code benchmarks across two open-source dLLM backbones, PACE-dLLM achieves the best average accuracy among the evaluated decoders on both backbones, with average throughput speedups of 5.23x on LLaDA and 3.06x on Dream (up to 8.52x on LLaDA MATH) over the unaccelerated semi-AR baseline, advancing the quality-throughput Pareto frontier.
